angle.","cites":["nyc-lpc","nyc-opendata"],"claim_ids":["c1","c8"],"slides":[{"title":"The Numbered Grid","body":"Jackson Heights sits within Queens's numbered street grid: avenues running east-west, streets running north-south. NYC Open Data's centerline layer maps 1,001 segments across the neighborhood, the skeleton that later open-space and housing patterns had to fit around.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Jackson Heights street centerlines, 1,001 segments mapped."},"claim_ids":["c8"]},{"title":"Broadway's Diagonal Cut","body":"Broadway ignores the numbered grid entirely. Its segments deviate about 37 degrees from the neighborhood's dominant axis, slicing diagonally through blocks and creating the triangular leftover lots that later became small plazas and garden entrances.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Broadway slices across the grid at roughly 37 degrees."},"claim_ids":["c1"]}]},{"title":"The Avenues That Hold the Line","intro":"Against Broadway's angle, the neighborhood's named avenues and streets stay locked to the grid, with deviations of a few tenths of a degree, and even the one exception falls just short of true diagonal.","cites":["nyc-opendata"],"claim_ids":["c2","c3","c4","c5","c6","c7"],"slides":[{"title":"Roosevelt Avenue & the El","body":"Roosevelt Avenue runs almost perfectly parallel to the grid, deviating only 0.2 degrees. Its width and straightness let the elevated IRT line run above it, making Roosevelt the commercial spine separating garden-apartment blocks to the north from denser blocks south.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Roosevelt Avenue aligned with the grid, carrying the elevated line."},"claim_ids":["c4"]},{"title":"Junction Blvd's Near Miss","body":"Junction Blvd deviates 14.5 degrees—more than any other named street except Broadway, yet still below the 15-degree threshold that would make it diagonal. It marks the neighborhood's eastern edge, where the strict grid begins to loosen.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Junction Blvd, the grid's closest call at the eastern edge."},"claim_ids":["c3"]},{"title":"Numbered Avenues as Backbone","body":"34 Avenue, 37 Avenue, Northern Boulevard, and 82 Street all deviate under one degree from the grid axis. These near-perfect alignments define the rectangular blocks that garden apartments and street trees were built to fit.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"34 Ave, 37 Ave, Northern Blvd, and 82 St tracing the grid."},"claim_ids":["c2","c5","c6","c7"]}]},{"title":"Wide Streets, Narrow Streets","intro":"The grid isn't uniform in scale: street widths vary widely across Jackson Heights, and that variation set the stage for which corridors could double as open space.","cites":["nyc-opendata"],"claim_ids":["c9","c10","c11"],"slides":[{"title":"Boulevards as Open-Space Corridors","body":"Street widths range from 6 to 70 feet. The widest, like Northern Boulevard, function almost as linear open spaces—room enough for planted medians, service roads, and the breathing room the dense apartment blocks lack internally.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"The widest street segments, up to 70 feet, act as green corridors."},"claim_ids":["c11"]},{"title":"The Narrowest Lanes","body":"At the narrow end, some service lanes measure just 6 feet wide—barely alleys. These slivers thread between buildings, leftover space the grid didn't fully absorb, often doubling as informal paths to interior courtyards.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Narrow 6-foot segments threading between buildings."},"claim_ids":["c10"]},{"title":"An Average Street","body":"Across all 1,001 mapped segments, the average street width is 32.6 feet—enough for two travel lanes, parking, and sidewalk planting strips that extend the neighborhood's green canopy without needing dedicated park land.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"A typical 32.6-foot residential street with planted sidewalks."},"claim_ids":["c9"]}]},{"title":"Gardens Behind the Grid","intro":"Where the grid left little room for public parks, Jackson Heights's developers built open space inward instead, carving shared gardens into the center of blocks the grid had defined.","cites":["nyc-lpc","city-lore","nyc-parks"],"claim_ids":[],"slides":[{"title":"Private Courtyards, Public Function","body":"Rather than relying on public parks, Jackson Heights's developers carved private interior courtyards into the center of each grid block—shared gardens accessible only to residents, substituting for the open space the dense grid otherwise lacked.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Interior courtyard gardens set within grid-defined blocks."},"claim_ids":[]},{"title":"Parks at the Edges","body":"Where the grid did yield public space, it followed block geometry: Travers Park's rectangular footprint matches the street grid's dimensions exactly, showing how open space and street layout were planned as one system, not two.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Travers Park, sized to the surrounding grid blocks."},"claim_ids":[]}]},{"title":"A Historic District Shaped by Both Systems","intro":"The interplay between Broadway's angle, the disciplined numbered grid, and the private gardens tucked inside it became the basis for landmark recognition of the whole neighborhood.","cites":["nyc-lpc","city-lore"],"claim_ids":["c1","c8"],"slides":[{"title":"Designation and Legacy","body":"The Landmarks Preservation Commission's historic district designation explicitly credits this pairing—a disciplined street grid interrupted by one diagonal, wrapped around private gardens—as what makes Jackson Heights distinct among New York's early planned communities.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"The historic district boundary over the street and garden pattern."},"claim_ids":["c1"]},{"title":"Reading the Map Today","body":"Together, the 1,001 mapped street segments and the courtyards, parks, and medians they enclose tell one story: a grid disciplined enough to organize growth, flexible enough to leave room for green space at every scale.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Jackson Heights's full street and open space system today."},"claim_ids":["c8"]}]}]}

gardens.","cites":["nyc-lpc","city-lore"],"claim_ids":["cl-count"],"slides":[{"title":"From Farmland to Grid","body":"In the early 1900s, the Queensboro Corporation carved Jackson Heights' farmland into a disciplined street grid. plan.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Major avenues aligned nearly perfectly with the neighborhood grid route.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Broadway crosses the neighborhood grid at a sharp diagonal angle."},"claim_ids":["cl-broadway"]},{"title":"Junction Blvd Stays True","body":"Junction Boulevard sounds diagonal, yet its path deviates only about 14.5 degrees from the grid, just under the threshold for a true crosscutting street, keeping it essentially grid-aligned.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Junction Boulevard's modest deviation keeps it within the grid-parallel range."},"claim_ids":["cl-junction"]}]},{"title":"Streets Meet Open Space","intro":"Street width wasn't uniform everywhere, and that variation left room for the courtyards and green buffers that define Jackson Heights' residential blocks.","cites":["nyc-parks","nyc-lpc"],"claim_ids":["cl-min-width","cl-max-width"],"slides":[{"title":"Widths that Make Room for Green","body":"Recorded widths range from 6 to 70 feet across the network, a spread wide enough to carry grand boulevards and narrow mews alike, each reserving room for green buffers beside buildings.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Street widths range from narrow mews to wide boulevards."},"claim_ids":["cl-min-width","cl-max-width"]},{"title":"Courtyards as Civic Space","body":"Behind narrower residential streets, garden apartment courtyards offered semi-private open space that city parks could not, letting the street network stay compact while green space lived mid-block instead.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Interior courtyards function as open space woven between narrow residential streets."},"claim_ids":[]}]},{"title":"A Legacy of Mutual Shaping","intro":"Jackson Heights endures as a case study in how a street system and an open space system can co-author a neighborhood's character over a century.","cites":["city-lore","nyc-opendata"],"claim_ids":[],"slides":[{"title":"Grid and Garden, Still in Dialogue","body":"A century later, Jackson Heights still reads as two overlapping systems: a near-perfect street grid interrupted once by Broadway, and a necklace of courtyards that grid made possible.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"The completed street and open space systems of Jackson Heights today."},"claim_ids":[]},{"title":"Why It Endures","body":"The lesson endures citywide: a disciplined street system does not crowd out open space, it can be the very framework that makes room for it, block by block.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Jackson Heights' street and open space profile as a model for planning."},"claim_ids":[]}]}]}
